zonenote: Every studio credited on each game, with the number of people credited under it. Eighteen studios carry their own color, either because they recur across games or because they brought a large crew to one. Every other chip takes its border color from the kind of work it did: development, testing, cinematic and sound, or publishing. Hover a chip to see the label. A dashed chip marked ∅ means the credits name a company but list nobody under it, as Halo 2 does with "ReelFX Creative Studios, Inc. - Additional Cinematic Animation". The company was credited, so the chip carries no number.
footnote: Treat these numbers as a guide rather than a record. They are read from published credit rolls by software, and credit rolls misspell names, omit people, and credit the same person twice. Some mistakes will have survived that. The dataset is here for insight into how the work was staffed, and it should not be used to settle who did what.

Halo Wars, Halo Wars 2, Halo: Spartan Assault, Halo: Spartan Strike and Halo: Fireteam Raven are out of scope. This project covers the twelve mainline campaign releases; the strategy and arcade spin-offs are a different dataset.

Credits come from each game's first release, so the Halo PC and Halo 2 Vista ports are left out and their teams are not counted. MCC is the exception, because 343 Industries published separate credit rolls for its later updates. Those rolls name their own people, so they are counted separately. The two ports may be represented anyway, without being named: Halo CEA was built on the Halo PC port, MCC was built on Halo CEA, and MCC took its Halo 2 from the Vista port. Some of the people credited under Halo CEA or TMCC (2014) may therefore have earned that credit on the earlier port work. The credits do not say, and this is not confirmed.

A remaster or collection does not inherit the original's credits as a new one. Combat Evolved Anniversary, both Master Chief Collection releases, and Campaign Evolved all reprint earlier rosters rather than re-crediting them: Combat Evolved's roll carries into all four; Combat Evolved Anniversary's own roll carries into both Master Chief Collection releases too, since MCC's own 'Combat Evolved' runs on Anniversary's remade assets rather than the 2001 original; Halo 2, Halo 3 and Halo 4's carry into both Master Chief Collection releases as well; Halo 3: ODST and Halo: Reach's carry into the 2018 one only; and TMCC (2014)'s own roll -- credit for the compilation itself, not any one game in it -- carries into the 2018 release too, since that one is an update to the same compilation rather than a new one. A name that appears only in a reprint keeps its original credit and gains no new one, but does get a small gold marker on the poster wherever the reprint sits, so the connection is still visible -- a dot for anyone credited elsewhere too, since their row already has room for it, or a badge on their one chip for someone credited on nothing else, since giving all of them a dot of their own would have meant giving each their own row. Either marker means the same thing: a reprint, not a fresh credit. It draws no line to anything, and a real credit that comes later still counts as a gap after it.

Publisher staff and community volunteers are both counted, and neither counts toward any developer or vendor figure, since both sat outside the team that built the game. On the grid neither carries a marker of its own any more: 'publisher staff' and 'community volunteers' are role classes like any other now, coloured and keyed the same way engineering or art are. Each game's card still gives them their own segment in the 'by employer' bar, since that bar reads the roster by who staffed people rather than by what they did. MCC's February 2025 update is entirely community: 50 Reclaimer volunteers, credited alongside no developers at all.

Vendor share is hard to compare across eras. Bungie-era credits carry almost no vendor tags while 343-era credits are full of them. Part of that is real growth in outsourcing and part of it is a change in how credits were written.
Voice actors credited for localized versions are left out. Only the original English cast is counted, so a game dubbed into ten languages does not read as having ten times the cast.

Role categories are a best guess and will not all be right. Where a credit names someone's job, that is what is used. Where it does not, the role is read from the heading the credit sat under, from a department printed beside the name, or from the same person's entry on MobyGames.
source: Source: Halopedia, Halo Waypoint, IGDB and MobyGames credit rolls. Official cover art, promotional art, game logos and studio logos courtesy of Bungie, Xbox Game Studios, 343 Industries, Halo Studios and the various artists who made them.
method: Every name here comes from a published credit roll. Four sources feed it: Halopedia, Halo Waypoint, IGDB and MobyGames. Each game is parsed into one row per credit, those rows are matched into people, and the people are laid out by which games they appear on. Nothing is sampled and nothing is estimated. If a name is on this sheet, a credit roll printed it. The same rules run over all twelve releases, so a comparison between two games compares the same measurement, and every figure is recomputed from the committed data on every build and checked against counts pinned in a test suite, so a change that quietly moves a number fails out loud. A credit roll is not a staff list, and that is the real limit here. It records who a studio chose to print, which is not the same as who did the work: people leave before a game ships and lose their credit, contractors appear under an agency rather than their own name, and whole disciplines are sometimes collapsed into a single line. Where the credits are silent, so is this. Matching people across twenty-five years is the other soft place. It is done by name, so two different people who share one are counted as one, and one person credited under two spellings is counted as two. Hundreds of those have been resolved by hand, and the ones that survive are the ones nobody has spotted yet. Roles carry a similar caveat, set out below: most are quoted from the credits, some are read from the heading a name sat under, and a few could not be worked out at all.
tools: Built in Python with Claude Code. The sheet is drawn as SVG and rendered to image with Playwright's headless Chromium, and NumPy and Pillow do the pixel work behind the cover art and the logos.
